blocks.content: India represents one of the 17 megadiverse nations, housing nearly eight percent of the world's species across ten distinct biogeographic zones.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: India harbors 4 of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots: The Himalayas, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland.
With only 2.4% of the world's land area, India accounts for nearly 7-8% of all recorded global species.
The country is classified into 10 distinct biogeographic zones ranging from Trans-Himalayas to Coastal and Island ecosystems.
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 established a three-tiered structure: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), State Biodiversity Boards (SBB), and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMC).

items: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) is a statutory autonomous body established in 2003 and headquartered in Chennai.
Sundaland hotspot includes the Nicobar group of islands, whereas the Indo-Burma hotspot covers the North-Eastern states south of Brahmaputra.
The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 provides the legal framework for establishing National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, unlike Biosphere Reserves which are declared under UNESCO's MAB programme.
